title: Occupancy hysteresis and paced-load experiments
content:
Purpose
This doc captures a set of experiments and an operational checklist for observing occupancy hysteresis and pacing effects in the serving runtime. We want repeatable ways to: (1) measure throughput/lossy-state when we rapidly change offered load, (2) quantify warmup time and priming artifacts (KV cache, allocator state, kernel selection), and (3) validate that client-side pacing mitigates transient congestion without hiding real bottlenecks.

Background / motivation
We repeatedly see runs where throughput after a burst does not return to expected steady-state immediately; GPU occupancy and internal queues appear sticky. Hypothesis: allocator fragmentation, kernel autotuner state, and KV cache warmness create hysteresis — the system's effective throughput depends on recent load history. This impacts capacity planning and makes SLA verification brittle unless we standardize priming/pacing.

High-level goals
- Design a minimal, repeatable harness to expose hysteresis across model variants (fp16/4bit/quant) and sequence-length mixes.
- Produce a reproducible warmup/decay protocol to quantify the time constants of recovery.
- Provide a recommended client pacing and measurement recipe for benchmark owners and SRE runbooks.

Key definitions (for clarity)
- Occupancy: measured GPU SM/TPC active fraction and device-side queue depth as inferred from NV counters.
- Hysteresis: difference in steady throughput after identical offered load depending on prior load history. Measured as relative throughput delta and recovery time constant.
- Priming: intentional early-phase traffic to populate KV cache, select kernels, and warm allocators.

Hypotheses to test
1) Short, high-intensity bursts create allocator fragmentation that reduces subsequent throughput for minutes unless compaction or process restart occurs.
2) Kernel autotuner caches chosen kernels per-shape; if subsequent traffic has different shapes, kernel-switch thrash causes high tail latency until caches settle.
3) KV cache warmness (prefix cache hit-rate) yields 10–40% token-cost reduction; cold starts amplify hysteresis.
4) Controlled client-side pacing (fixed inter-arrival jitter + max concurrency) reduces observed p99 spikes and makes steady throughput more stable for benchmarking.

Experiment matrix (variables)
- Model variant: base fp16, quantized int4, LLM-medium, LLM-large
- Sequence length distribution: short (mean 64), mixed (mean 256), long (mean 1024)
- Burst profile: microburst (100ms high rps), plateau (sustained 10m), staircase (ramp 0->50->0->50 RPS)
- Warmup primer: none, short primer (2 minutes at 20% target load), aggressive primer (10 minutes at 70% target load)
- Client pacing policy: open-loop (max concurrency), closed-loop (feedback: keep p95 latency under target), fixed inter-arrival (Poisson with controlled CV)
- Thermal baseline: cold (after 30m idle), hot (after 1h 80% occupancy)

Measurement targets and signals
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for token generation and overall request end-to-end
- Throughput: tokens/sec and requests/sec measured at client and server (to detect queueing)
- GPU metrics: SM utilization, memory utilization, PCIe bandwidth, GPU temperature, power
- Host metrics: CPU steal, scheduling delay, network TX/RX, process RSS/allocator churn (mmap stats)
- Runtime internals: KV cache hit rate, kernel selection log counts, number of active worker threads, internal queue lengths, batch sizes distribution
- Traces: end-to-end traces with span tags for: client-send, client-retry, ingress-queue, scheduling, inference-start, kernel-runtime, inference-end, egress-serialize

Load generator configs (example recipes)
1) Staircase experiment (good for hysteresis mapping):
- Steps: 0% -> 25% -> 50% -> 75% -> 50% -> 25% -> 0%
- Step duration: 5 minutes
- Inter-arrival model: Poisson with mean inter-arrival = 1/RPS, CV target 1.1 (add jitter)
- Concurrency cap: set to target concurrency inferred from desired latency SLO
- Seed hygiene: fix RNG seeds for prompt sampling and tokenization so workloads are identical across runs

2) Microburst test (exposes transient throttling/backpressure):
- Pattern: 10 bursts per minute, burst length 200ms, peak RPS 5–10x baseline
- Baseline between bursts: 50% of peak
- Repeat 20 minutes

3) Priming comparison runs:
- Cold run: start from idle, no priming, measure time-to-stable throughput
- Short primer: 2 min priming at 25% of target tokens/sec using frequent short prompts
- Aggressive primer: 10 min warmup at 70% target using mix of prompts that exercise long sequences

Instrumentation and profiling steps
- Lightweight runs: enable only runtime counters (KV hits, batch sizes) and host/GPU metrics to reduce noise.
- Heavy profiling: for runs where we see hysteresis, capture GPU traces (nvtx annotations, CUPTI) for a 60s window post-change. Also capture perf samples on the main worker threads for 60s.
- Kernel selection logging: toggle debug flag to emit kernel-hash -> chosen-kernel mapping, roll-up counts
- Allocator introspection: sample allocator stats (free lists, mmap count) every 10s during the experiment.
- Tracing sampling: sample 1/10 of requests for full distributed trace to avoid trace overhead.

Repeatability checklist (pre-run)
- Node prep: reboot GPU nodes at least 30 min before critical long experiment or follow thermal stabilization procedure.
- Process state: kill & restart service processes unless experiment explicitly needs retained process state. Document exact git commit and runtime binary.
- RNG seeds: set seeds in loadgen for prompt selection. Attach seed file to artifacts.
- Workload artifacts: store prompt set, tokenizer version, prompt preprocessor version.
- Environment: record driver/cuda/cuDNN/NCCL versions, kernel, BIOS, and cloud image id.
- Monitoring baseline: capture 5m of idle metrics before starting.

Run sequencing and cadence
- Warm-up phase: 10 minutes of low-intensity traffic (5–15% target) with the same input distribution as the experiment to let tokenizers, caches, and jitters settle.
- Baseline capture: 5 minutes of steady 25% traffic to capture nominal metrics.
- Perturbation phase: run the staircase or bursts while capturing high-resolution telemetry.
- Decay phase: return to 0–5% traffic and capture 15 minutes to observe recovery.

Data analysis guidance
- Compute hysteresis metric H = (steady_throughput_after_down - steady_throughput_after_up) / steady_throughput_expected. Report H per-model and per-seqlen mix.
- Fit recovery to exponential: throughput(t) = A + B * exp(-t/tau). Extract tau (time constant) with bootstrap confidence intervals.
- Correlate tau with allocator churn (mmap/s), kernel-switch counts, and KV cache hit-rate delta.
- Produce heatmaps: H across (sequence-length, primer-duration) grid and tau across (model-variant, burst-severity).

Troubleshooting notes
- If run-to-run variance is high: check for noisy multi-tenant co-tenants on the same host, kernel driver preemption, or cloud hypervisor activity. Re-run on isolated GPUs.
- If KV hit-rate remains low after aggressive primer: validate primers’ prompt prefixes match expected request prefixes (we likely primed wrong tokens).
- If tail latency spikes persist despite pacing: inspect internal queuing (ingress/batching queues) and backpressure behavior. Pacing can mask resource shortages, so pair pacing experiments with resource-limited runs.

Operational recommendations (for benchmark owners)
- Standard benchmark recipe: 10m warmup (5–15% load), 5m baseline at 25%, perturbation (staircase) 30m, decay capture 15m. Store full artifact bundle.
- Always publish seed file, prompt set, tokenizer version, binary SHA, and environment manifest with any throughput claims.
- If hysteresis H > 5% for expected steady-state, flag for deeper profiling and consider adding a library-level compaction or scheduled low-latency compaction sweep.

Open questions / notes to self
- How much of the hysteresis is due to NUMA/locality effects when batching grows/shrinks — add a NUMA-aware microprofile next.
- Can we safely perform allocator compaction in prod without latency regressions during compaction? Need a canary.
- Should we expose a runtime endpoint to query kernel-cache fingerprints and explicit compaction trigger?

Artifacts to attach to PRs
- raw-metrics.tar.gz (prometheus samples, nvidia-smi logs, perf traces)
- seed.json and promptset.txt
- kernel-selection.log and allocator-samples.csv
- generated plots: hysteresis-heatmap.png, recovery-tau-curve.pdf

Quick run recipe (one-liner to reproduce locally)
- docker run --rm -e TARGET_RPS=50 -v $(pwd)/prompts:/prompts redwood/loadbench:canary --pattern=staircase --seeds=seed.json --out artifacts/run-$(date +%Y%m%d)-stair.json

References
- CONFLUENCE-1234 (hysteresis theory and prior experiments)
- GitHub PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/loadbench/pull/212 (pacing client)
